source.title: Steering Large Language Models between Code Execution and Textual Reasoning
source.authors: Yong-Chao Chen; Harsh Jhamtani; Srinagesh Sharma; Chu-Chu Fan; Chi Wang

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some table and figure layouts are flattened, and numerical values for the plotted success rates are not given in the text.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares downstream task success across different models and reports cases where smaller models outperform larger ones. This is a different measure from held-out pretraining loss or compute-optimal allocation, but bears on downstream predictability (V6).
record.gate_note: The study does not measure held-out cross-entropy loss, sweep parameter count, training tokens or compute, fit scaling laws, or test compute-optimal allocations. Those claims, and claims about architecture shape and other training regimes, are not tested. Its relevant results are downstream task success rates and stated comparisons across model sizes in the Code Interpreter setting. Other results comparing steering methods or reporting token and runtime costs do not test the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study compares downstream task success across GPT models of different (unstated) size under Code Interpreter. It reports smaller models beating GPT-4o on two tasks and calls this inverse to Kaplan scaling. This is a new tool-augmented setting bearing on V6. It is not a controlled scale sweep: parameter counts are not given, and the models differ in training as well as size.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors find no single code/text steering method is best across 14 tasks and 6 models, and forcing code does not guarantee better accuracy. With Code Interpreter, smaller GPT models sometimes beat larger ones on Number Multiplying and Game 24. They attribute this inverse scaling to larger models' overconfidence in textual reasoning. Their proposed Code+Text+Sum method performs best on average but costs more tokens and runtime.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates downstream task success across existing models and steering methods; it does not train models or fit pretraining-loss scaling laws.
record.method_sensitivity: Task complexity and model choice affect success and code-use patterns; the paper also reports that steering method and prompt choices affect task outcomes.

fits_no_version.finding: Larger GPT models with Code Interpreter choose textual reasoning over code more often, and their code more often resembles text reasoning.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Tool-use propensity, and hence tool-augmented task accuracy, can fall with model scale.

record.problems: The study does not report parameter counts or relate performance to pretraining loss. Some relevant success-rate comparisons are available only as plots, without exact values in the text. The model-size comparisons cover selected models and tasks rather than a controlled scale sweep.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant results left out. Other steering-method and task results do not measure model-size predictability.

untested.parts: Pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
Extrapolation of fitted laws to larger runs.
Architecture shape effects at fixed parameter count.
Relation of downstream performance to pretraining loss; any controlled sweep over known parameter counts or compute.
Dependence of fitted exponents or splits on setup and fitting choices.

missing.what: Average normalized scores across 14 tasks per model and method. Larger models (GPT-4o, O1-preview) generally score above GPT-4o-mini and GPT-3.5.
Exact Code Interpreter success rates for Number Multiplying (84/100/100) and Game 24 (18/62/92) for GPT-4o/GPT-4o-mini/GPT-3.5.
Pure-text Number Multiplying accuracy across four OpenAI models (GPT-3.5 to O1) by task complexity. All fail as complexity grows.

record.verdict_notes: The record wrongly states that exact success rates are absent; the appendix tables give them. The inverse-scaling result is narrow, confined to two tasks with tool use. The model comparison confounds size with training differences, and parameter counts are never stated.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens or compute.
Whether fits on small runs predict losses of much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation and its trend with compute.
Effects of depth, width and other architecture choices on loss at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer.
The paper reports task accuracy across selected models and tasks, but does not relate it to pretraining loss or quantify a general predictive relationship over parameter counts.
The study does not fit exponents or compute-optimal splits, or test how those fits depend on counting, schedules, data or fitting method.

relationships.condition: Code Interpreter on Number Multiplying and Game 24, GPT-4o vs GPT-4o-mini vs GPT-3.5
relationships.reason: Smaller models outperform GPT-4o on both tasks: Number Multiplying 100/100 vs 84, Game 24 92/62 vs 18. The authors attribute this to larger models choosing text over code (r1, r4-r9). Sizes are unstated and the models are not a controlled sweep.
relationships.display_finding: GPT-4o-mini and GPT-3.5 scored 100 and 100 versus GPT-4o's 84 on Number Multiplying, and 92 and 62 versus 18 on Game 24, attributed to GPT-4o favoring text over code.

relationships.condition: Average normalized score over 14 tasks, most steering methods including Code Interpreter
relationships.reason: Based on the text, since no row records it. Table 2 shows the larger or newer models scoring higher on average: e.g. Code Interpreter 83.5 GPT-4o, 80.8 GPT-4o-mini, 64.5 GPT-3.5. The inverse ordering is confined to specific tasks.
relationships.display_finding: Larger or newer models score higher on average under most steering methods, with Code Interpreter scores of 83.5 for GPT-4o, 80.8 for GPT-4o-mini and 64.5 for GPT-3.5, despite reversals on specific tasks.
